newsitem.title: BRAZIL: South America's largest city acts to cut smog.
newsitem.headline: South America's largest city acts to cut smog.

text.p: Residents of South America's largest and most polluted city should breathe a little easier after the state government on Monday imposed a traffic plan to cut emission levels in smog-choked Sao Paulo.

For a second straight year, Sao Paulo state's Environmental Secretariat implemented a plan to cut by 20 percent the 3.4 million motor vehicles that circulate on the metropolitan area's congested roads each day.
"Last year's (plan) was successful and this year we've extended the programme," a state spokesman said.

The plan, which restricts motor vehicles based on their license plate numbers from circulating between 7 a.m. and 8 p.m. one day a week, lasted less than a month last year. This year it will extend through August.
State workers, wearing protective masks over noses and mouths, stood at street corners and handed out some tickets but said motorists appeared generally to support the plan.
The impact of the car rotation scheme on Monday was felt immediately, especially by traffic-weary drivers.
"Traffic has improved a lot," taxi driver Geraldo Tello said.. "There seems to be more cooperation this year."

Brazil's industrial heartland, greater Sao Paulo is home to more than 16.5 million people, over 10 percent of the country's population, and 5.7 million motor vehicles are registered in the metropolitan area.
The traffic rotation plan is intended to take 650,000 cars off streets each work day, state officials said.

"The idea is to improve the quality of life," the state spokesman said. "The programme has increased the speed of the traffic flow and has improved traffic but the main purpose is to improve air quality.
The dry Southern Hemisphere winter months of June through August are the most polluted due to convection currents resulting from cold air masses and the lack of cleansing rains, officials said.
Scientists and doctors blame the severe pollution during Sao Paulo's winter for a host of respiratory problems, skin ailments and pregnancy complications.
Newspaper polls last year found that 90 percent of motorists back the traffic plan, despite the inconvenience and fines of $100 to $1,900.
Similar steps have been taken in Mexico City and Santiago, Chile, two other Latin American cities burdened by severe smog.
